newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-VAN ROOYEN THREATENS LIONS TOUR.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-VAN ROOYEN THREATENS LIONS TOUR.

text.p: Former South African rugby union officials on Saturday threatened to try to stop the forthcoming British Lions tour if their grievances with the current administration are not resolved.

Brian van Rooyen and several members of the former South African Rugby Union (SARU) called on the South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) to address their grievances or risk repercussions for the Lions tour, which begins in May.

"We will give SARFU a deadline to resolve the various problems with the administration and development of rugby in this country and we will also take up the matter with the Ministry of Sport," van Rooyen told Reuters.

"Should this fail, we will then go to the International Rugby Football Board (IRFB) to stop the British Lions tour of South Africa later this year, and all other international tours here, until everything has been resolved.
"We are not a splinter group but dissatisfied SARFU members who want to hold the controlling body for the sport in this country to the promises they made at the time of unification."
Van Rooyen, a former Transvaal Rugby Union vice-president, spoke after a five-hour meeting with around 50 former SARU players and administrators at the Perseverance College of Education on Saturday.
The meeting elected a seven-man coordinating committee to liaise with SARFU and to air several grievances.
"Our grievances mainly concern amateur rugby in the townships, racism and the development programme," van Rooyen said.
"Rugby in the townships needs to be addressed because the game there is dying. Clubs from the disadvantaged areas frequently disband due to lack of games and funds."
Van Rooyen said that, since rugby union had become professional, genuine amateur rugby had been neglected.
"Racism also still exists in player selection and in the lack of equality. There is a lack of genuine development programmes and financial support in the disadvantaged areas."

Magmoed Efferdi from the Western Cape, who is on the new committee, said: "To talk the truth doesn't need a mandate and development in South Africa is a swear word. White rugby has returned to the international scene on the backs of the former black unions."

Northern Cape's Jim Summers, also elected on to the committee, said: "This should be an investment for the future of rugby and we must establish a culture of rugby in the dying areas. We are certain to be labelled rebels in rugby -- but rebels with a cause. And that cause is proper unification at all levels."
